value.A3i6E: The Master of Science (MS) in Laboratory Animal Science (MLAS) program in the Department of Comparative Medicine is a two-year graduate degree designed to prepare students for advanced careers in laboratory animal science, biomedical research, and related scientific fields. The curriculum provides comprehensive training in animal modeling and biomethodology, laboratory animal science, regulatory compliance, animal husbandry and welfare, organizational management, and research facility design. Students gain a strong academic foundation through interdisciplinary coursework while developing the technical, analytical, and professional skills needed to contribute to the advancement of biomedical research. Graduates are well prepared for careers in academia, biotechnology, pharmaceutical and biomedical industries, and research institutions, or for continued education in medical, veterinary, or other advanced graduate programs. Advanced Hands-On Learning in Biomedical Research The MLAS program emphasizes experiential learning by integrating classroom instruction with practical hands-on experiences. Students work alongside leading faculty, researchers, and senior staff, applying scientific principles in real-world laboratory settings while developing critical thinking, problem-solving, and research skills. NEW FOR 2027: Two Program Pathways Beginning with the 2027 cohort, the MLAS program offers two distinct academic pathways: a thesis track and a non-thesis track. This allows students to select the experience that best aligns with their career goals and professional interests. Thesis Track The traditional Thesis Track is designed for students seeking an in-depth research experience. Students are matched with a faculty mentor at the beginning of the program and remain in that laboratory throughout their degree. Working closely with their mentor, students develop and execute an independent research project that culminates in the completion and defense of a master's thesis. This pathway is ideal for students interested in research-intensive careers or pursuing advanced graduate degrees. Non-Thesis Track The Non-Thesis Track provides a broader experiential learning model for students interested in exploring multiple areas of laboratory animal science and biomedical research. Rather than completing a single, long-term research project, students participate in a series of quarter-long applied projects across a variety of disciplines and settings. Projects may be completed within Stanford laboratories as well as with partnering organizations, providing exposure to diverse research environments, technologies, and professional opportunities. This pathway emphasizes practical experience, professional development, and workforce readiness for careers across academia, industry, and research support organizations. It is ideal for students interested in pursuing advanced professional degrees (including veterinary and medical education and training) or who are exploring careers in research support areas such as regulatory compliance, biomedical research facility operations and management, animal husbandry and welfare, and investigator education and training. Applicants must indicate their preferred pathway—Thesis Track or Non-Thesis Track—at the time of application.
value.ItCSB: The Master of Science in Laboratory Animal Science (MLAS) program equips students with the scientific knowledge, technical expertise, and professional competencies needed to excel in laboratory animal science and biomedical research. Through rigorous coursework, hands-on learning, and individualized training, students develop a strong foundation in animal modeling and biomethodology, laboratory animal science, regulatory compliance, animal welfare, and research methodologies. Graduates are prepared to: Apply scientific principles and best practices in laboratory animal science and biomedical research. Design, conduct, and evaluate research using ethical and scientifically rigorous methodologies. Demonstrate knowledge of animal welfare, regulatory compliance, and responsible research practices. Communicate scientific findings effectively through written, oral, and professional presentations. Collaborate effectively in interdisciplinary research and laboratory environments. Apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills to address complex challenges in biomedical research. Students may tailor their educational experience by selecting either the Thesis Track , which emphasizes independent research under the guidance of a faculty mentor, or the Non-Thesis Track , which provides hands-on experience through a series of applied projects across diverse research settings. Both pathways prepare graduates for careers in academia, biotechnology, pharmaceutical and biomedical industries, and research institutions, as well as for advanced study in medical, veterinary, or graduate programs.
value.advisingExpectations: Academic Advising The MLAS program is committed to providing a collaborative and supportive advising experience that fosters academic achievement, professional growth, and career development. Upon admission, students are paired with advisors based on their selected program pathway. Thesis Track : Students are matched with a faculty advisor whose research interests align with their academic and professional goals. This faculty mentor serves as the student's primary research advisor throughout the program, providing guidance on research design, thesis development, academic planning, and career preparation. Non-Thesis Track : Students are advised by the Student Services Officer, Program Director, and designated program faculty, who provide guidance on academic planning, professional development, and the successful completion of quarter-long applied projects. Students may also work with project supervisors at Stanford or partnering organizations during individual project rotations. All students are required to meet with Faculty advisors and Student Services Officer at least once each quarter to review academic progress, discuss professional goals, and support the development of the student's Individual Development Plan (IDP). Students and advisors are encouraged to meet regularly throughout the year to discuss coursework, research or project experiences, career exploration, and professional development opportunities. Successful advising is a shared responsibility. Students are expected to actively engage in the advising relationship by seeking guidance, communicating regularly with their advisor or mentor, and maintaining familiarity with program policies, degree requirements, and academic milestones. To foster a productive mentoring relationship, students and advisors should periodically review expectations and maintain open, respectful, and professional communication. The Student Services Officer monitors each student's academic progress and the completion of program requirements. Detailed information regarding degree requirements, academic milestones, and advising expectations is available throughout the program website and MLAS Handbook In addition to faculty mentorship, students are encouraged to work closely with the department's Student Services Officer, who can connect them with Stanford resources that support academic success, career planning, health and wellness, and professional development. Additionally, the program adheres to the advising guidelines and responsibilities listed by the Office of the Vice Provost for Graduate Education (VPGE), at Graduate Academic Policies (GAP), and at Graduate Advising . For more information regarding Graduate Student Advising and Postdoctoral/Resident Mentoring, contact the following people: Graduate Student Advising: Venessa Juarez (Student Services Officer), venessaj@stanford.edu Program Director: Megan Albertelli (Comparative Medicine Chair), megan.albertelli@stanford.edu Program Co-Director: Jose Vilches-Moure, jvilches@stanford.edu Postdoctoral Student/Residents: David Bentzel (Laboratory Animal Medicine Residency Director), dbentzel@stanford.edu Postdoctoral/Resident: Katherine Gates (Resident and Trainee Wellness Advisor), kvgates@stanford.edu

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Advanced Courses
published_requirement_narratives.text: ​​Our program embraces the highly interdisciplinary nature of neuroscience research by allowing students to create an individualized curriculum of advanced topic courses best suited to their research agenda and scientific development needs. This approach has empowered students to take advantage of the breadth of expertise across the university. A minimum of six credits of Advanced Topics coursework is required of each student. Students select the courses while meeting the following criteria: (1) at least one course must be taken with a minimum of three units, (2) the course must have a clear means of evaluation (i.e., problem sets, paper writing, class presentations), and (3) the student must detail how the course relates to the student’s project or domain of neuroscience. This information is submitted in writing along with the course syllabus and examples of problem sets to the co-directors/curriculum committee co-chairs for approval. Six units of advanced neuroscience coursework are required. To complete the six units, at least one course must be three units or more; the remaining units can be completed with a combination of smaller-unit courses (e.g., 3+2+1, 3+2+2, 4+2). Pre-approval for advanced courses is required. Required courses must be taken for a letter grade and passed with a 3.0 (B) or better.

published_requirement_narratives.heading: Master's Thesis Defense
published_requirement_narratives.text: MS Students will write a proposal in the style of an NIH NRSA proposal and a written rigor document which outlines how the proposed research has addressed NIH's four key areas of rigor as well as a plan for dissemination for research outcomes and products. The student will defend the proposal and rigor document by oral presentation to the Master's thesis committee. The student will complete the proposed Master's thesis project and defend the project through an oral presentation to the Master's thesis committee. The student must defend the thesis project through oral presentation to the Master's thesis committee by the end of the 2nd year.

value.A3i6E: Master’s in Translational Medicine (M-TRAM) is a professional degree program that trains students to advance promising biomedical solutions from early-stage research to full regulatory approval. Technology focus areas include immunotherapy, gene therapy, vaccines, biomarkers, single-cell omics, and medical devices. M-TRAM combines flexible classroom learning with hands-on, team-based medical research, one-on-one mentoring by renowned Stanford faculty and investigators, and on-site biotechnology training. M-TRAM focuses on three integrated areas representing key stages of translational medicine. Rather than specializing in only one area, students develop strong working knowledge across all three domains throughout the program: Early Translation: Basic Science to Preclinical Clinical Translation: Clinical Investigation Late Translation: Medical Adoption and Commercialization There are two complementary M-TRAM Tracks based on the type of capstone project students pursue: TRIP (Translational Research Individual Project) : track requiring a faculty-mentored individual capstone research project . TEAM (Translation, Entrepreneurship, and Applied Medicine Project) : track requiring a collaborative team-based capstone project , organized by therapeutic or focus area. TRIP and TEAM track students have overlapping but separate coursework requirements, as indicated here: https://med.stanford.edu/m-tram/academics/schedules.html

value.ItCSB: By the end of the one-year program, students will have gained the problem-solving skills, competencies, and strategies: Expand professional networks and career opportunities Develop a complete product development plan encompassing pre-clinical, clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory modules Identify unmet medical needs Develop scientific hypotheses Design clinical studies Apply clinical specimens to emerging technologies Understand research design, methodology, data analysis, data reporting
